1.5 Everyday use

Once the default config names a source folder and a plugin, these are the only commands you need:

diskproxy start      # or just: diskproxy
diskproxy status
diskproxy stop

start launches the server in the background, waits for it to scan the folder, mounts the result and prints where:

Ready: /Volumes/DiskProxy
Select this volume in your application (under Disks in PMP).
After use: diskproxy stop

Closing the Terminal window does not stop the view. status prints the server’s process ID and the mounted volume. stop finishes any pending capture, unmounts, then stops the server and deletes the session folder.

Each config file has its own view, so several can run at once, such as a photo library and a camera card. --config FILE selects the view for start, status and stop; without it, start uses the default config, status lists every running view, and stop stops the only one or, when several are running, names them and asks for --config. A second start of the same config is refused while its view runs.

1.5.1 Choosing a source or config for one session

A path after start overrides the configured source. --config selects another config file, before or after start, and --set overrides any single key:

diskproxy start /another/folder
diskproxy --config ~/views/library.json start
diskproxy start --config ~/views/library.json --set label=Library

1.5.2 Scanning large folders

Before it can serve a disk, the server reads the whole tree. For a camera card this takes a moment. For a large library the launcher shows progress on one line, updated in place every two seconds:

Scanning: listing folders: 3120 folders, 905000 files
Scanning: reading files: 523000 of 1256465 (41%)

The server logs a summary when it finishes, for example scanned 1256465 files in 2413 folders in 59 s. The launcher waits up to 15 minutes while the server is alive, and stops at once if the server exits with an error. Short scans print nothing. When output is not a terminal, each update is printed on its own line.

Measured on one library, a tree of 1.26 million files scanned in about a minute; the server then used about 1.2 GB of memory, with a 1.8 GB peak during startup. With camera metadata spliced into its 566,000 JPEGs (see the previews plugin below), the same tree scanned in 110 seconds and used 1.9 GB, with a 2.5 GB peak. A second library of 835,383 preview JPEGs, all but 440 with metadata from a 3.8 GB metadata store, scanned in 111 seconds on a busy machine and then used 1.64 GB. Trees of up to 8 million entries are supported.

1.5.3 When the volume is busy

If an application still has files open, macOS refuses to detach the disk, and stop says so and leaves the server running, so the application can finish. Close the files and run diskproxy stop again. Before detaching, stop checks that the mounted volume is still the one it attached, by its volume UUID, so it never detaches some other disk.

1.5.4 The session folder

Each view’s session lives in ~/Library/Caches/diskproxy/sessions/NAME, where NAME is its config file’s name without .json (set DISKPROXY_STATE_DIR to move the parent folder). It holds the server’s startup JSON and error log, the process ID and start time, the attachment details and, for writable views, the shadow file or overlay and the harvester’s log. A session started by an older launcher in ~/Library/Caches/diskproxy/session is still found, as the default config’s view.
